events.prelimNarrative: On October 18, 2026, about 1500 central daylight time, a Piper J3C-65 airplane, N88218, was involved in an accident near Boonville, Indiana. The pilot was not injured and a passenger in a vehicle that was struck by the airplane was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 91 personal flight. The pilot reported that he departed from runway 9 at the Boonville Airport (I91), and shortly afterward returned to make a low approach to runway 27. He flew in ground effect until reaching the west end of the runway where he climbed, performed an “impossible turn,” and glided toward runway 9. He then applied full throttle when he was on short final for runway 9 and entered a climbing right turn to establish the airplane on a left downwind for runway 27. He then made a descending 180° turn to final approach. The approach was steep and carried the airplane down the runway. The pilot flew in ground effect with minimal throttle until about 2/3 of the way down the runway where he applied full throttle. He kept the airplane in ground effect as airspeed increased. When at the departure end of runway 27 and still at a low altitude, the airplane impacted a car traveling northbound on South Baker Road, which passed along the west edge of the airport. The pilot stated that he did not see the car traveling northbound until it was in front of him due to tall weeds, shadows cast on the road by trees, and the dark color of the car. He attempted to pull up to avoid the collision but was not able to. The airplane continued to fly, and the pilot circled the airport for about 2 hours before landing on runway 9. The pilot estimated that the airplane’s speed was about 70 mph at the time of the impact. The pilot reported no preimpact mechanical anomalies that would have precluded normal operation. The left main landing gear was separated from the airplane during the impact. The right side of the car was impacted and damaged. The passenger of the car, who was seated in the front right seat was transported to the hospital with serious injuries and later succumbed to those injuries. The driver of the car and the pilot were not injured.

events.prelimNarrative: On October 13, 2026, about 2130 central daylight time, a Piper Aircraft PA-46-350P JetProp DLX airplane, N931TT, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Reedsburg, Wisconsin. The pilot, the pilot-rated passenger, and the four passengers sustained fatal injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 91 personal cross-country flight. The pilot was the owner of the airplane, and the purpose of the flight was to transport friends to a sporting event and back home. A preliminary review of flight track data showed that on the day of the accident, the airplane departed the Menomonie Municipal Airport (LUM), Menomonie, Wisconsin, about 1443. The airplane landed at the Kenosha Regional Airport (ENW), Kenosha, Wisconsin, about 1548. The pilot filed an instrument flight rules flight plan, and the airplane departed from ENW about 2043, with a destination as LUM. The flight track data showed that the airplane departed from ENW and flew to the northwest, then turned to a west heading and climbed to a cruise altitude of flight level (FL) 240. The pilot was issued the weather conditions along the route of flight. At 2125, the pilot, who was in contact with the Chicago Air Route Traffic Control Center (ZAU ARTCC), reported the airplane had encountered icing conditions, and requested a lower altitude. The pilot was approved to descend the airplane to an altitude of 11,000 ft. The ZAU ARTCC controller made several attempts to assist the pilot after the pilot stated the airplane was having issues with the radios, and the pilot was unsure of the airplane’s heading, altitude, and airspeed. The controller lost communications with the airplane as it descended through 15,000 ft. The flight track data showed the airplane initially continued in a west direction and entered into a right-hand descending turn, with upward pitch changes, and a rapid increase in airspeed reaching as high as 339 kts, before decreasing. The airplane briefly ended up on a track about 180° in the opposite direction, until the flight track data was lost about 2130. A preliminary review of weather information revealed that the National Weather Service Aviation Weather Center Current Icing Product indicated an area of 50 percent probability of icing conditions existed at FL 240 in the vicinity of the accident site, near the time of the accident. The icing severity indicated pockets of light to moderate icing were possible in the vicinity of the accident site. A preliminary review of archived information showed the pilot did not request weather information from Leidos Flight Service. The pilot did have an account through ForeFlight, and he did receive a weather briefing from ForeFlight. The debris path was located throughout a rural residential area and the Mirror Lake Pine Oak Forest State Natural Area, owned and managed by the state of Wisconsin. Both areas consisted of large trees and heavy brush. There were no ground injuries or property damage. Both wings were found separated from the fuselage. Both horizontal stabilizers and elevators were found separated from the empennage. The wreckage was documented at multiple locations, it was recovered from the accident site, and it was transported to a secure location for future examination. Multiple damaged avionics units were removed from the airplane and were transported to the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory. The airplane, which was manufactured in 2008, was equipped with a Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6A-35 turboprop engine and a MT-Propeller MTV-16-1 four-blade, controllable pitch, wood and composite propeller. The airplane was originally manufactured and known as a Malibu Mirage, but was later converted in November 2019 to a JetProp DLX model through an FAA supplemental type certificate held by the Rocket Engineering Corporation. The airplane was also equipped with an autopilot system. The pilot held an airline transport pilot certificate with ratings for airplane multi-engine land, airplane single engine land, and a type rating for the Embraer EMB-500 Phenom 100 airplanes. The pilot successfully completed a 14 CFR 61.58 pilot-in-command proficiency check on September 17, 2026, in an Embraer EMB-500 Phenom 100 airplane. The pilot-rated passenger held a commercial pilot certificate with ratings for airplane multi-engine land, airplane single engine land, and instrument airplane. He also held a flight instructor certificate with a rating for airplane single engine land. A review of the airplane’s maintenance records showed the airframe, the engine, and the propeller all had an annual inspection performed by a mechanic on November 13, 2025. A review of the JetProp DLX Pilot’s Operating Handbook and FAA-Approved Airplane Flight Manual states that the airplane may be operated in day or night visual flight rules, day or night instrument flight rules, and known icing when the appropriate equipment is installed and operable. This document states to monitor the ambient air temperate and that while severe icing may form at temperatures as cold as -18° Celsius (-0.4 Fahrenheit), increased vigilance is warranted at temperatures around freezing with visible moisture present. The document also contains a warning about operating in severe icing and states: Severe icing may result from environmental conditions outside of those for which the airplane is certificated. Flight in freezing rain, freezing drizzle, or mixed icing conditions (supercooled liquid water and ice crystals) may result in ice build-up on protected surfaces exceeding the capability of the ice protection system, or may result in ice forming aft of the protected surfaces. This ice may not be shed using the ice protection systems and may seriously degrade the performance and controllability of the airplane.

events.prelimNarrative: On October 12, 2026, about 1513 central daylight time, a Monnett Sonerai 2LT airplane, N473AS, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Sextonville, Wisconsin. The pilot was seriously injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 test flight. The owner reported that the accident flight was the first flight of the recently completed amateur-built airplane. Shortly after takeoff, about 300 ft above ground level, a plume of black smoke was observed from the engine compartment, and the airplane lost all engine power. The airplane impacted a swamp resulting in substantial damage to the fuselage and both wings. The airplane was retained for further examination.

On October 10, 2026, about 2014 Pacific daylight time, a Piper PA-18-150, N927JS, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Wauconda, Washington. The flight instructor and student pilot were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the pilots’ family members, the student pilot had recently purchased the airplane, and had planned to fly the airplane from Willow Airport (PAUO) Willow, Alaska, to Kamiah Municipal Airport (S73), Kamiah, Idaho. According to an itinerary the student pilot had sent to family members, he anticipated it would take 3-4 days to fly from PAUO to S73. Both pilots booked commercial airline flights to Anchorage, Alaska, before departing PAUO on the morning of October 7, 2026. Between October 7 and October 9, the pilots performed several intermediate stops until they reached Prince George Airport (CYXS), Prince George, British Columbia, Canada, on the evening of October 9. At 0739 on the morning of the accident, the student pilot texted a family member, stating they were waiting for fog to lift before they departed. At 0808, he texted again, stating they were departing soon, but would have to divert around localized areas of fog. At 0914, he texted that they were departing CYXS. At about 1944, the student pilot sent a text indicating that they had landed at Dorothy Scott International Airport (0S7), Oroville, Washington, and were about to depart for the last leg of the flight to Kamiah Municipal Airport (S73), Kamiah, Idaho. According to preliminary air traffic control data provided by the FAA, one of the pilots of the accident airplane contacted Seattle Air Route Traffic Control Center (ZSE) to report they were about 10 miles south of 0S7 and were requesting flight following. The controller at ZSE provided the pilots with a transponder squawk code and asked about the flight’s destination. The pilots replied they were flying to Idaho County Airport (GIC), Grangeville, Idaho. About three minutes later, ZSE reported they had radar contact with N927JS about 20 miles southeast of 0S7 and asked for the airplane’s altitude. The pilots responded they were at 8,000 ft. About one minute later, ZSE attempted to reach the pilots because they had lost radar contact. The pilots did not respond, and no further radio transmissions were received from the airplane. When ZSE was unable to reestablish radar or radio contact with the airplane, the FAA issued an ALNOT. According to the Okanogan County Sheriff's Office, the airplane was located the following evening on the west face of Mount Annie, about 21 miles northeast of Omak, Washington. The main wreckage came to rest on forested, upsloping terrain at an altitude of about 5,069 ft above mean sea level. Examination of the accident site revealed a wreckage path that was about 225 ft long and generally oriented on a magnetic heading of 089°. The first identified points of contact (FIPC) were the tops of two tall fir trees which had been severed. About 120 feet east of the FIPC, sections of both wings were found about 40 feet above the ground, wrapped around the trunks of two fir trees. Both main landing gear, the inboard ends of both wings, freshly broken branches, and fragments of clear plastic were distributed along the ground near the end of the wreckage path. The main wreckage, which included the cabin, wing struts, engine, propeller, and empennage, came to rest nose down with the engine buried in the soil and the empennage folded down and to the right. The throttle levers were found positioned fully forward, the mixture knob was found in the full rich position, the primer pump was in and secure, the fuel selector was positioned to the right fuel tank, and the carburetor heat knob was set to off. An engine data monitor was removed from the airplane and retained for readout of any stored data. Further examination of the wreckage is pending following recovery.

events.prelimNarrative: On October 7, 2026, at 0952 central daylight time, an Lancair IV-P airplane, N5SV, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Haslet, Texas. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) part 91 personal flight. A review of commercially available Automatic Dependent Surveillance Broadcast (ADS-B) data revealed that the flight departed Hicks Airfield (T67), Fort Worth, Texas, about 0951. ADS-B data showed that the airplane climbed to 875 ft mean sea level (msl) before it entered a left turn. The airplane climbed to 1,000 ft msl and slowed to 84 kts ground speed before it descended (Figure 1) Figure 1. N5SV Flight Track The airplane impacted power lines along the south side of a roadway. Fragments of composite propeller, fiberglass, and acrylic pieces were found under the power lines. An impact ground scar started about 3 ft from the north edge of the roadway and continued about 6 ft into an adjacent ditch. An impact crater along with fiberglass debris were located in the bottom of the ditch about 20 ft southwest of the main wreckage. Fire damage to grass and vegetation was observed upslope from the crater. The main wreckage came to rest upright on the north side of the ditch. It consisted of the fuselage, both wings, engine, and portions of the propeller. The fuselage was aligned along a true heading of 304°. A postimpact fire consumed a majority of the main wreckage. The horizontal stabilizer and elevator assembly separated from the aft fuselage and came to rest against a brick privacy wall north of the main wreckage. The vertical stabilizer and rudder assembly also separated from the aft fuselage and came to rest at the same privacy wall. The empennage exhibited no evidence of thermal damage. The wreckage was transported to a secure location for further examination.

On October 7, 2026, about 1038 Pacific daylight time, an experimental amateur built Vans RV-7A, N425DG, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Petaluma, California. The pilot and flight instructor were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight. According to a family member, the flight instructor was conducting a flight review with the pilot. Preliminary ADS-B flight track data showed that the airplane departed from runway 29 at Petaluma Municipal Airport (O69), Petaluma, California, about 1037:29. The airplane climbed to about 300 ft above ground level (agl) and accelerated to a ground speed of about 89 knots. The airplane crossed the departure end of runway 29 about 1037:55, at about 300 ft agl and a ground speed of 84 knots. About 1037:58, the airplane entered a turn to the right and maintained an approximate altitude of 300 ft agl, with brief altitude oscillations. The airplane’s ground speed continued to decelerate until the end of the ADS-B data. At 1038:10, the data showed the airplane in a descent at about 200 ft agl and a ground speed of 63 knots. (See figure 1.) A review of security camera footage located at O69 showed the airplane on upwind for runway 29 in a climb attitude, until it leveled off and subsequently began a turn to the right. The airplane remained at about the same altitude in the right turn. About 9 seconds after the start of the turn, the airplane’s angle of bank increased and it descended in a nose down attitude into terrain. According to a witness located near the departure end of runway 29, he heard the airplane departing and did not look up, initially. He then heard what sounded to him like an engine “backfire” and walked out of his hangar to look. He observed the accident airplane in a right bank and stated that the bank angle continued to increase. Subsequently, the airplane rolled to the left and “fell straight down” until it impacted the ground where a postcrash fire ensued. Figure 1. Preliminary ADS-B flight track data Examination of the accident site revealed that the airplane impacted an open field at an elevation of about 118 ft mean sea level (msl) about 1,300 ft north of the departure end of runway 29. The wreckage debris path was about 63 ft in length, about 60 ft wide and oriented on a magnetic heading of about 154° from the first identified point of contact (FIPC) to the main wreckage. The FIPC was a depression in the ground about 6 ft wide, 8 ft long, and about 2 ft deep. The propeller was separated from the engine slightly aft of the propeller flange and located about 57 ft northwest of the main wreckage. All 6 propeller bolts remained attached to the propeller flange. The airplane’s canopy was observed about 59 ft southwest of the main wreckage. The main wreckage came to rest upright on a magnetic heading of about 299°and displayed extensive thermal damage. All major structural components of the airplane were located throughout the debris path. The wreckage was recovered to a secure location for further examination.

On October 7, 2026, at 1021 eastern daylight time, a Cessna 525 airplane, N600AL, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Bedford, Pennsylvania. One airline transport pilot sustained minor injuries, and the other airline transport pilot sustained serious injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 positioning flight. The flight crew reported that they arrived at the departure airport and the first officer completed a preflight inspection of the airplane. The crew reported that preflight, engine start, and taxi were uneventful. They continued that the airplane accelerated normally during the takeoff roll. The captain, who was the pilot flying, reported that during the takeoff roll the controls felt heavier than normal and as the airplane reached rotation speed it didn’t “fly itself off the ground.” He then attempted to rotate and reported that the nose bounced at least once. The first officer reported that, during the takeoff roll, the captain stated he couldn’t lift the nose. The captain continued that the resistance on the yoke increased as the speed of the airplane increased. The captain subsequently made the decision to abort the takeoff and applied the brakes. The first officer stated that he deployed the speed brakes when the captain called for the aborted takeoff. The airplane departed the runway surface, crossed a grassy area, went through the airport perimeter fence, and came to rest in a field across from the airport. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage, both wings, and was partially consumed by postaccident fire. The airplane was retained for further examination.

On October 06, 2026, at about 1653 eastern daylight time, a Hughes 269B, N9390F, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Lahmansville, West Virginia. The pilot was fatally injured. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. A witness reported that the pilot performed an extensive preflight inspection and engine runup check. The helicopter lifted off at 1645 and departed from runway 06 of the private airstrip. The helicopter entered the right traffic pattern and completed two low approaches down the runway. During the third upwind climb, the witness observed that the helicopter appeared to ascend at a lower rate and entered a slight descent as it transitioned to downwind. Shortly afterward, the witness lost sight of the helicopter due to the terrain. Another witness performing an agricultural operation about 1/2 mile southeast of the airport reported that helicopter overflew his property during the first two passes, as it transitioned from downwind to the base leg of the traffic pattern. During the third pass, the helicopter performed a 180° turn at an altitude of about 150 ft above ground level and maneuvered to a field about 1/4 mile northeast of his location. He observed the helicopter’s tailboom make a “quick wag” as it appeared to enter a hover, followed by a high rate of descent in an upright position. The witness noted that he did not hear the engine or see the impact due to operating equipment and terrain. One witness reported the helicopter’s engine sound was “loud and of consistent tone.” Another witness reported the engine as having a “slight misfire” as it flew over his property. The accident site was located about 1/2 mile east of the private airstrip in about a 9° sloped grass field adjacent to a roadway. The debris path was about 124 ft in length and oriented on a magnetic heading of 060°at an elevation of 1,050 ft. There was an odor of fuel present, and the grass surrounding the main wreckage exhibited fuel blight. Ground impressions consistent with the impact of the tailrotor and skids revealed the helicopter impacted the ground in about a 17° nose-up attitude and came to rest on its right side about 15 ft from the point of impact and oriented on a magnetic heading of 136°. A soil depression observed between the linear skid impressions contained residual engine oil and fragments of the engine oil sump. All components of the helicopter were accounted for at the accident site. The tailboom was separated from the fuselage. The two tailrotor blades were undamaged and remained attached to the hub, with no anomalies noted to their pitch change links or swashplate. No anomalies were noted to the tailrotor gearbox during hand rotation of the rotor blades, and oil was visible in the sight glass. The tailrotor driveshaft was separated from impact forces about 19 inches from its drive pulley coupler and deformed upward about 3 inches from the tailrotor gearbox. The drive shaft exhibited torsional deformation between 37 to 50 inches from the tailrotor gearbox. The tailrotor pitch-change remained attached to its mounts and impact separated about 10 inches from the fuselage bellcrank. The lower fuselage was crushed upward and the canopy was fragmented. The pilot’s four-point restraint was latched, and its inertia real was locked with the webbing separated from impact forces. The restraint’s lower outboard attached point was pulled from the fuselage. The pilot’s seat frame was deformed downward and fractured. The fuel control was in the ON position, and the magneto switch was on BOTH. The electric fuel pump was ON, and the mixture control was partially leaned. The rotor clutch switch was engaged and in the locked position. The battery and generator switches were noted in the ON positions. Continuity of the cyclic and collective controls were established from the cockpit controls to the main rotor head. Control continuity was established from the cockpit antitorque pedals to the bellcrank and through impact separated control tube to the tailrotor blades. Continuity of the throttle cable was confirmed from the collective to the impact fractured bellcrank assembly. The collective’s throttle control friction was engaged and could not be released by hand. There was no impact damage noted to the collective control. The main rotor gearbox housing remained attached to the bottom of the main rotor mast and to the center frame. The gearbox lower housing was fractured from impact forces and oil was present in the assembly. The main gearbox rotated freely, and continuity was established from the drive pulley to the rotor head. The lower drive pulley was partially separated from its support structure, and its input shaft remained engaged in the pulley and attached to the engine. The drive belts were intact and partially separated from the pulleys. The freewheeling (one-way) sprag clutch operated correctly and its supporting structure was fractured from impact forces. The sprag clutch actuator cable remained attached to the sprag clutch and the linear actuator. The three main rotor blades were secured to their respective grips, which remained attached to the main rotor head and mast. The red rotor blade was relatively straight with slight skin buckling observed, and its trim attach point pulled inward. The blue rotor blade was bent downward about 9 inches from its attach point and downward deformation about mid-span with light chord-wise abrasion noted to its outboard area. The yellow rotor blade was bent downward about 9 inches from its attached point and exhibited skin buckling and chord-wise abrasion at its outboard area. A material consistent to that of a body filler was observed on the lower blade skin’s outboard area. Sections of the filler were separated and were not located at the accident site. The damage noted to the rotor blades were consistent with low rotor rpm at ground contact. The fuel tank was breached at its outboard manufactured seam and a semicircle impression with linear transfer marks consistent with impact from the main rotor drive pulley and belts was observed to its inboard area. The fuel cap remained attached to its receptacle, and vent and pick-up screen were clear of debris. Fuel line continuity was established from the fuel servo to the fuel tank through impact fractured fuel lines. Fuel was observed in the gascolator, and its filter was clear of debris. The electric fuel pump was determined to be functional during field test with a power source. The engine remained attached to its mounts and exhibited impact damage to upper crankcase area. The oil sump was fragmented, and the induction air filter was crushed. The oil pump suction screen and pressure filter media were clear of debris. The exhaust and induction tubes were crushed. The fuel and oil lines remained attached to their respective attachments. The engine driven fuel pump exhibited impact damage and fuel was observed within the pump. The fuel servo was impacted separated from the engine. The throttle was observed in the closed/idle position, and the control cable rod end was fractured from the servo. The mixture was observed in the rich position, and its control cable was pulled from its fuel servo attachment. Fuel was observed in the servo, and its fuel inlet screen was clear of debris. Impact damage was noted to the fuel injector lines, and the injectors were clear of debris. Both magnetos remained attached to the engine and produced spark from their ignition towers during rotation of their drive gears. The sparkplug electrodes were intact and exhibited normal wear and coloration. Initial rotation of the crankshaft beyond about 90° was unsuccessful. Disassembly of the engine revealed impact deformation noted to the crankcase precluded camshaft rotation. There were no preaccident anomalies noted to the crankshaft, main bearings, or oil system. The connecting rods remained attached to their respective crank pins and rotated freely. The interior of the cylinders, pistons, rings, and valves were unremarkable. The wreckage was retained for further examination.

On October 4, 2026, about 2130 mountain daylight time, a Diamond Aircraft DA-40 airplane, N162GL, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Eldorado Springs, Colorado. The pilot and passenger were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. ADS-B data indicated that the flight departed from runway 29 at the Vance Brand Airport (LMO), Longmont, Colorado, about 1832. The pilot initially proceeded west and then south from LMO and maneuvered southwest of Boulder at altitudes up to 12,000 ft mean sea level (msl). He then flew about 68 miles to the northwest before reversing course, reaching altitudes of up to 15,000 ft msl during that portion of the flight. About 2036, the pilot returned to the vicinity of Boulder and maneuvered in that area between about 11,000 ft msl and 7,500 ft msl. The final ADS-B data point was recorded at 2129:39 and located about 1 mile north of Eldorado Springs. The altitude corresponding to that data point was about 7,375 ft msl. The Search and Rescue Satellite-Aided Tracking (SARSAT) network detected the airplane’s emergency locator transmitter (ELT) signal at 2131. Notification of that signal was received by the Air Force Rescue Coordination Center (AFRCC) at 2132. The Boulder County Sheriff’s Office was notified of the active ELT signal at 2143, and a search subsequently located the accident site about 1016 the following morning. The site was in mountainous terrain about 1 mile west of the final data point at an approximate elevation of 7,360 ft. The airplane impacted rising terrain about 300 ft below a ridgeline. The airframe was fragmented. Due to the difficulty of the terrain, and for safety reasons, the NTSB did not respond to the accident site. Airframe and engine examinations will be conducted after the wreckage is recovered to a secure location.

events.prelimNarrative: On September 30, 2026, about 1946 Pacific daylight time, a Eurocopter Deutschland GMBH EC-135 P2+, N313RX, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Avalon, California. The pilot, flight nurse, and patient were fatally injured; the flight paramedic was seriously injured, and the passenger sustained minor injuries. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 135 air medical flight. The helicopter departed Pebbly Beach Seaplane Base (L11), Avalon, California, with a planned destination of Torrance, California. A review of ADS-B data revealed that the helicopter climbed to a maximum altitude of about 90 ft mean sea level. Shortly thereafter, the helicopter entered a descent for several seconds before it impacted water. The last data point indicated the helicopter’s groundspeed was about 65 knots, and its descent rate was about 1,280 fpm. Witnesses near L11 reported that the helicopter lifted off from the seaplane base, entered a descent and then impacted water. The witnesses also noted that it was a dark, moonless night. A review of surveillance video revealed that a medical helicopter operated by another organization departed L11 about 45 seconds before the accident helicopter. The video showed that the helicopter lifted off from its helipad into a hover, turned and departed to the north. Approximately 13 seconds later the helicopter entered a descent, contacted the water twice, and then entered a climb. The accident helicopter then lifted off, climbed slightly and departed on a northerly heading. Several seconds later the helicopter entered a nose low attitude and subsequently impacted the water about 8 seconds later. The helicopter wreckage was located in the water, at a depth of about 209 ft, about 0.3 miles north of L11. The wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.

On October 1, 2026, about 1450 Pacific daylight time, an experimental amateur built Glasair FT airplane, N314SR, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Everett, Washington. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to friends of the pilot, before departure from Snohomish County Airport, Everett, Washington (KPAE) the pilot removed the upper and lower engine cowling to replace the exhaust gas temperature probe and Hobbs meter. FAA ADS-B data did not capture the accident flight. Video of the departure showed the airplane take off from runway 34L and begin rolling left almost immediately after liftoff. During the initial climb, the left bank continued to steepen until the airplane disappeared from view into trees west of the runway. A witness reported that the airplane initially appeared level and climbed at a normal rate. Within a few seconds, it entered a left bank that became substantially steeper than a normal departure turn. The witness estimated that the airplane climbed no higher than about 100 to 150 ft above ground level and described the turn as smooth rather than abrupt or erratic. The airplane remained in the banked turn until it disappeared behind trees. The witness did not observe the impact and did not recall unusual engine sounds, smoke, or components separating from the airplane before it disappeared from view. Another witness reported seeing the airplane about 50 to 60 ft above ground level in a steep left bank over the west side of the airport. The airplane continued in the banked turn until it disappeared into a wooded area. The controller reported hearing an unintelligible radio transmission that appeared to be from the pilot during the turn. The controller stated that the engine sounded normal before it disappeared from view. The main wreckage was located in a wooded area about 1,100 ft west of runway 34L and exhibited extensive impact and fire damage. The first identified point of impact was a tree crown that had separated about 75 ft above ground level, about 150 ft northeast of the main wreckage. The left wingtip was located beneath this tree strike, and additional material from the left wing was distributed between that location and the main wreckage. Both ailerons were present and exhibited thermal damage. Examination established flight control continuity from the control stick to the right aileron and to portions of the left aileron control system. An intermediate section of the left aileron push-pull tube had separated and was thermally damaged. The forward and aft wing spars were significantly damaged in that area. Elevator control continuity was established from the control stick to behind the seat. Thermal damage aft of that location precluded confirmation of continuity to the elevator. The rudder cables were continuous to the bell crank, which remained connected to the pushrod associated with the rudder. The flap handle was engaged in the third of four detents. The fuel selector handle was found in the wing tank position. The throttle and mixture controls were fully forward, the primer was pushed in and locked, and the ignition switch was in the BOTH position. The engine was rotated manually using the propeller. Rotational continuity to the magnetos and valve train movement were established, and thumb compression and suction were obtained on all four cylinders. Cylinder No. 1 was removed, and the exposed internal components exhibited no visible anomalies. Both magnetos exhibited thermal damage and water/foam intrusion; normal operation of both magnetos was not verified. The carburetor bowl was separated from the upper assembly, and the floats were deformed. The wreckage was retained for further examination.

On September 29, 2026, at about 1347 eastern daylight time, a Smith Pitts Special S-1, N292Y, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Madison, Georgia. The pilot was seriously injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the pilot, on the day of the accident, he planned to fly from Madison Municipal Airport (52A), Madison, Georgia, to Atlanta Regional Airport-Falcon Field (FFC), Atlanta, Georgia to retrieve an airplane part. The pilot indicated the flight from 52A to FFC was uneventful, and after obtaining the airplane part, he departed for the return flight to 52A. Shortly after the pilot began his descent toward 52A, the airplane suddenly experienced a total loss of engine power. The pilot turned on the airplane’s fuel boost pump, but when that failed to restore engine power, he began looking for a suitable area to perform a forced landing. As the pilot maneuvered the airplane toward a clearing, the engine briefly “revved up” two or three times before losing power again. The pilot subsequently performed a forced landing in the front yard of a residence. During the landing roll, the airplane impacted a tree, resulting in substantial damage to the wings and empennage. The pilot stated that, after he extracted himself from the airplane, he saw fuel pouring out of the airplane’s fuel tank. The airplane was recovered to a secure storage facility for examination.

On September 27, 2026, about 1608 central daylight time, an experimental PA-18 Replica airplane, N43LK, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Buffalo, Minnesota. The pilot was fatally injured, and the pilot-rated passenger was seriously injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. A witness reported that the airplane took off from runway 18 and appeared to be climbing at a steep angle. He described the engine sound as “loud.” Shortly afterward, the airplane rolled off and entered a steep descent before impacting the ground. Figure 1 – Airplane at accident site. Initial ground impressions were consistent with a nose-down impact at the north edge of taxiway A1. The airplane came to rest at the taxiway A1 hold short line which was about 27 ft southwest from the initial impact and oriented on a southeast heading. The wings were dislocated and resting in position relative to the fuselage. Both wings exhibited leading edge crushing damage along the entire span. The engine was displaced upward relative to the fuselage, and the cockpit area was compromised. The aft fuselage was oriented upward with the empennage intact. The flight control surfaces remained attached to the airframe. The control cables were secured to the respective control surfaces. They were continuous to the wing roots, for the ailerons and flaps, and to the cockpit area for the elevators and rudder. Flight control cable separations were retained for further examination. FAA records revealed that the airplane was issued an experimental special airworthiness certificate on June 25, 2026. The records listed no flight time (0.0 hours) for the airplane as a newly constructed aircraft when the certificate was issued. Current flight time for the airplane was not available at the time of accident. FAA records also revealed that the pilot was issued a private pilot certificate on August 12, 2026. At that time, he had logged 75.8 hours total flight time with 17.2 hours of pilot-in-command and 5.2 hours of tailwheel airplane flight time. His logbook contained a tailwheel airplane endorsement. No flight time was logged subsequent to the issuance of his private pilot certificate.

On September 27, 2026, about 1202 Pacific daylight time, an experimental amateur-built Bearhawk Patrol, N240BP, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Cottage Grove, Oregon. The pilot sustained serious injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot reported that, during the initial climb at an altitude of approximately 2,300 ft mean sea level (msl), he reduced the propeller speed from 2,650 rpm to 2,500 rpm. Immediately thereafter, he thought the engine had an uncontained failure and components had struck the windscreen, which obstructed his forward visibility. Using his view through the left side window, the pilot maneuvered toward a suitable off-airport landing area. During the descent, the stall warning horn activated, and the pilot lowered the airplane’s nose and continued the approach to a field. The airplane subsequently touched down on uneven grassy terrain and came to rest upright. Post accident examination of the airplane revealed that the fuselage was substantially damaged. The engine cowling was displaced upward and aft, onto the windscreen. No visible holes were observed within the engine crankcase. The 2 bladed constant speed propeller remained attached to the engine crankshaft; however, one of the two blades was separated from the propeller hub and was not located at the accident site. The airplane was recovered to a secure location for further examination.

On September 26, 2026, about 1120 eastern daylight time, an Aero Commander 112, N1102J, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Chatsworth, Georgia. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the pilot’s wife, the purpose of the flight was to reposition the airplane from Martin Campbell Field (1A3), Copperhill, Tennessee, to Dalton Municipal Airport (DNN), Dalton, Georgia. She stated that she dropped the pilot off at 1A3 on the morning of the accident about 0930 so that he could pick up the airplane from maintenance. She recalled that the pilot had taken the airplane for maintenance after the pilot heard an audible warning noise related to the left main landing gear after turning on the airplane electrical power. She stated that the mechanic believed it was a switch, so he sprayed the switch with a water displacing chemical and then cycled the landing gear several times. On the morning before the flight, the mechanic had planned to cycle the landing gear one last time before the pilot took the airplane to DNN. According to ADS-B data provided by the FAA, the airplane departed from 1A3 at 1056 and flew toward the south. The airplane then turned toward the west at 1103 and continue toward DNN. The airplane’s final ADS-B observed position was recorded at 1110, with the airplane at an altitude of 4,600 ft mean sea level (msl) and located about 11 miles east of DNN. The accident site was located in a small hay field about 1 mile southeast of DNN, and there were no known witnesses to the accident. The wreckage was examined at the accident site. The right fuel tank was breached, and the fuel selector was observed in between the right fuel tank and off positions. Air was blown through the right fuel line at the wing root, through the fuel selector to the firewall with no blockages observed. Fuel was present at the firewall when air was applied to the right fuel system line. The fuel strainer was impact-separated from the airplane. Fuel was found within the fuel injector unit. The fuel manifold did not contain any debris and the fuel lines to the fuel injectors were secure. The fuel injectors were unobstructed. The engine-driven fuel pump, oil filter, and fuel injector unit were impact-separated from the engine. The engine’s crankshaft was rotated by hand when force was applied to the crankshaft flange. Thumb compression and suction were observed on all four cylinders, valve action movement was observed, and continuity of the crankshaft to the camshaft was observed throughout the engine. The engine cylinders were examined with a lighted borescope and no anomalies were observed. No evidence of any preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures of the engine were observed. The airplane was equipped with a two-blade, controllable-pitch propeller. One propeller blade remained straight and was undamaged. The second blade was bent aft about 8 inches from the tip. Video footage obtained from first responders showed that fuel was visibly leaking steadily from the right fuel tank when they arrived at the accident site. According to the mechanic who had performed the most recent maintenance of the airplane, the airplane had consistently had small problems since the pilot purchased it. Most recently, the pilot was having a problem starting the engine. The mechanic flow-tested the fuel injector nozzles and found that they were not flowing evenly, so he replaced them with new nozzles. During the fuel nozzle troubleshooting, the mechanic removed a piece of debris, similar to silicone, from the fuel injector line. The pilot also had a problem starting the engine on a recent flight that was attributed to the Bendix drive on the starter not engaging, so he replaced the starter. Most recently, and in the days prior to the accident flight, the pilot reported to him that when he turned on electrical power, he immediately saw and heard the left main landing gear unlocked indication and horn. The mechanic attributed it to a sticking switch, so he sprayed it with a water displacing spray and cycled the gear several times. He then left the airplane on jacks and cycled the gear one last time on morning of the accident flight. The mechanic added that during the engine runup, he radioed to the pilot that if he had a left gear unlocked indication during the flight, it was likely just that switch, and that he should not be concerned. The mechanic provided a fuel receipt that showed the pilot had obtained 35.6 gallons of 100LL the day prior to the flight. Audio of the DNN common traffic advisory frequency was obtained from a security camera mounted in the lobby of the airport that also captured radio traffic. The audio included radio calls from the accident pilot, and no distress calls could be heard. Flight logbooks for the pilot were reviewed, but no entries were made after June 21, 2026. The pilot’s wife stated that the pilot flew several times after the last logbook entry date. At the time of the last logbook entry, the pilot recorded a total of 125.7 hours. He had accumulated a total of 14.9 hours in the accident airplane as of the last recorded logbook entry. The pilot received his complex airplane endorsement on July 15, 2025. The wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.

On September 23, 2026, about 1711 Pacific daylight time, a Cessna 172B, N44P, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Royal City, Washington. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the pilot’s family, he departed from a private airstrip on his property at about 1630. Shortly thereafter, a worker at a farm located near B & G Farms Airport (4WA0), Royal City, Washington, saw the airplane land on runway 7. The worker periodically turned his attention to the airplane and saw it back-taxi to the approach end of runway 7 and stand with the engine running for about 20 minutes. The witness saw the airplane taxi in one or two circles before it lined up with runway 7 and began its departure roll. The airplane’s takeoff appeared normal until it rotated into a nose high pitch attitude as it passed a building located alongside the runway. The airplane began to climb steeply, yawed left, and overflew a road and residence. The airplane then rolled to the left, its nose dropped, and it subsequently impacted a farm field about 450 ft north of the runway. (See figure.) The witness stated he could hear the airplane’s engine running during the entire flight without any irregularities or changes in tone. Figure: A depiction of airplane’s flight path, as described by the witness. The airplane came to rest inverted on an approximate magnetic heading of 070°. The first identified point of impact was a divot in soft mud that contained fragments of the landing and taxi light lens from the left wing. The left wing was crushed aft outboard of the lift strut, and mud had adhered to the leading edge. The right wing leading edge was crushed aft. Both flaps appeared to be in the retracted position. The engine, engine mount, and firewall were displaced aft. The pilot’s seat was separated from the seat rails and the seat pins were bent. The seat rails were partially separated from the floor, and one seat rail was bent around the seat base roller assembly. The wreckage was retained for further examination.

On September 24, 2026, about 0945 Pacific daylight time, an Aeronca 7AC, N12DF, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Hesperia, California. The flight instructor and passenger were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. According to the operator of the airplane, the pilot had rented the airplane and departed from Apple Valley Airport (APV), Apple Valley, California, on the day of the accident flight. A destination was not offered by the pilot, just a basic query as to where to go for breakfast. The accident was witnessed by multiple people within the vicinity of the accident site. One witness stated that due to construction equipment, they could not hear the airplane, however, they noticed a small airplane flying in the area. They recalled that the tail appeared lower than the wings with the tail moving laterally from right to left before the airplane rolled over and he was able to see the belly of the airplane. The airplane’s nose was pointed down and then he saw the airplane descend toward terrain. Examination of the accident site revealed that the airplane impacted terrain about 1.5 miles southwest of Hesperia Airport (L26), Hesperia, California. The airplane came to rest in a nose down attitude, in open desert terrain on a heading of about 160° magnetic, at an elevation of 3,584 ft mean seal level (msl). There was no visible ground scar observed surrounding the wreckage. The propeller assembly and propeller blades remained attached to the engine and the engine was pushed aft toward the firewall. The undercarriage of the cockpit was crushed forward toward the engine, with the empennage and tail at an almost 90° degree angle. Both wings remained attached to the fuselage and had sustained leading edge crush damage throughout. The airplane was recovered to a secure facility for further examination.

On September 23, 2026, about 1755 central daylight time, an experimental Magni M16 gyroplane, N109MG, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Annapolis, Missouri. The pilot and passenger were both fatally injured. The gyroplane was operated under the provisions of Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 as a personal flight. First responders located the gyroplane and reported it had collided with power lines and impacted terrain. A power outage in the area was also reported. FAA inspectors responded to the accident scene and examined the wreckage. The debris field, which began with separated sections of the pusher propeller, was about 100 yards in length. Portions of the horizontal stabilizer and rudder system were located about midway through the debris field. A ground scar consistent with ground collision was found about 10 to 15 yards north of the main wreckage, surrounded by fragments of windscreen, airframe pieces, and rotor blades. The gyroplane came to rest on its left side, and cyclic and rudder control continuity appeared to be continuous. Fuel was observed in the fuel tank. A power line was entangled in the main wreckage. The gyroplane was retained for further examination.
